extractions.value: The above patient had most of the classical features of the stiff-man syndrome: onset in middle age; stiffness initially involving the trunk muscles with persistence of rigidity even at rest; superimposed painful spasms precipitated by stress and exertion; hyperlordosis of lumbar spine with restricted forward flexion; gradual progression over months; otherwise normal neurological examination with normal higher functions, motor power, sensations and reflexes; characteristic EMG changes of continuous normal motor unit activity at rest in affected muscles with no signs of denervation or primary muscle disease and normal nerve conduction studies. The presence of GAD and islet-cell antibodies in our patient supports the hypothesis of an autoimmune basis for the pathogenesis of the syndrome.

The presence of GAD and islet-cell antibodies in our patient supports the hypothesis of an autoimmune basis for the pathogenesis of the syndrome.

The above patient had most of the classical features of the stiff-man syndrome: onset in middle age; stiffness initially involving the trunk muscles with persistence of rigidity even at rest; superimposed painful spasms precipitated by stress and exertion; hyperlordosis of lumbar spine with restricted forward flexion; gradual progression over months; otherwise normal neurological examination with normal higher functions, motor power, sensations and reflexes; characteristic EMG changes of continuous normal motor unit activity at rest in affected muscles with no signs of denervation or primary muscle disease and normal nerve conduction studies.

Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies were strongly positive in both serum and CSF and islet cell antibodies were present in serum at high titres (> 80 Juvenile Diabetes Foundation Units - normal < 10).

Electromyography studies did not show any changes of a primary muscle disease but there were spontaneous normal motor unit potentials over the abdominal and paraspinal muscles even at rest which decreased after intravenous administration of diazepam. The silent period and nerve conduction studies were normal.

The patient was started on diazepam and baclofen, the doses of which were progressively increased to 30 and 60 mg per day respectively. With this, there was a significant decrease in the muscle rigidity and spasm, the lumbar lordosis decreased and the scoliosis disappeared.
Routine blood and urine tests and imaging studies of the abdomen were normal.

Extrapyramidal syndromes like torsion dystonias, progressive encephalomyelitis, spinal cord lesions, localized tetanus, Issac's syndrome and myotonia can closely mimic the stiff-man syndrome. These and other local pathologies like peritonitis can be differentiated by the classical features of the disease together with electrophysiological studies but a high index of suspicion is also required in the early stages.
